text: From around 3000 B C. <break time="0.8s" /> The Sumerian officials would mark their lists of goods. <break time="0.8s" /> On clay tablets. <break time="0.8s" /> If they wanted to record five fish. <break time="0.8s" /> They would mark five pictures of a fish. <break time="0.8s" /> Their first great intellectual leap came. <break time="0.8s" /> From separating the number from the object they were counting. <break time="0.8s" /> In other words. <break time="0.8s" /> They would represent five fish. <break time="0.8s" /> With a numeral for the number five. <break time="0.8s" /> Alongside a symbol for the fish. <break time="0.8s" /> If they wanted to describe five of something else. <break time="0.8s" /> They realized. <break time="0.8s" /> They could keep the same numeral. <break time="0.8s" /> And trade the object symbol. <break time="0.8s" /> For a cow, or a jar of oil. <break time="0.8s" /> Or whatever else they were interested in. <break time="0.8s" /> The Sumerians had developed the idea of an emancipated number. <break time="0.8s" /> Existing in its own right. <break time="0.8s" /> And independent of whatever it is being used to count. <break time="0.8s" /> It is easy to take the emancipated number for granted. <break time="0.8s" /> As it is so deeply set into modern thought. <break time="0.8s" /> But to the earliest civilizations. <break time="0.8s" /> It was intellectually new and extremely powerful.
